units.title: Raster and Vector Graphics
units.tip: Graphics come in two fundamentally different forms. Raster graphics are made of pixels arranged in a grid, while vector graphics are made of mathematical shapes like lines and curves. Each has strengths depending on the task.

exercises.question: What is a raster image?
exercises.answer: An image made of a grid of colored pixels
exercises.explain: Raster images are composed of pixels arranged in rows and columns. Each pixel has a color value. Photos and screenshots are raster images.
choices: An image without any color information
An image made of mathematical curves
An image made of a grid of colored pixels

exercises.question: What happens when you scale up (enlarge) a raster image?
exercises.answer: It becomes pixelated and loses detail
exercises.explain: Raster images have a fixed number of pixels. Enlarging them spreads the same pixels over more space, causing visible pixelation and blurriness.
choices: It becomes pixelated and loses detail
It automatically adds new pixels smoothly

exercises.question: Which file formats are raster-based?
exercises.answer: JPEG, PNG, and GIF
exercises.explain: JPEG, PNG, and GIF all store images as grids of pixels. SVG and PDF are vector formats.

exercises.question: What is the resolution of a raster image?
exercises.answer: The width and height measured in pixels
exercises.explain: Resolution is specified as width x height in pixels, like 1920x1080. Higher resolution means more pixels and more detail.
choices: How many colors the image contains
How sharp the camera lens was
The width and height measured in pixels

exercises.question: How much storage does an uncompressed raster image need?
exercises.answer: Roughly width x height x bytes-per-pixel
exercises.explain: A 1000x1000 pixel image with 3 bytes per pixel (RGB) needs about 3 megabytes before compression. Larger images need proportionally more storage.
choices: Roughly width x height x bytes-per-pixel
Only dependent on the file format

exercises.question: What is a vector graphic?
exercises.answer: An image defined by mathematical shapes and curves
exercises.explain: Vector graphics store instructions for drawing shapes, lines, and curves mathematically. Logos and fonts are typically vector graphics.
choices: An image made of colored pixels
An image defined by mathematical shapes and curves

exercises.question: What happens when you scale a vector graphic?
exercises.answer: It scales smoothly with no loss of quality
exercises.explain: Vector graphics are recalculated at any size. A vector logo looks perfect at any scale from business card to billboard.
choices: It scales smoothly with no loss of quality

exercises.question: What are common vector file formats?
exercises.answer: SVG, PDF, and AI
exercises.explain: SVG is the web standard for vector graphics. PDF and AI (Adobe Illustrator) are also vector formats. PNG and JPEG are raster formats.

exercises.question: What is a 'path' in vector graphics?
exercises.answer: A line or curve defined by mathematical points and control handles
exercises.explain: Paths are the basic building blocks of vector graphics. They are drawn between anchor points and can be curved or straight.
choices: A line or curve defined by mathematical points and control handles
A saved version of the image

exercises.question: Which is better for a company logo: raster or vector?
exercises.answer: Vector, because it scales infinitely without quality loss
exercises.explain: Logos need to work at any size. Vector graphics maintain perfect quality when scaled, making them ideal for branding.
choices: It depends on the monitor size
Vector, because it scales infinitely without quality loss

units.title: Pixels and Color Models
units.tip: Pixels are the building blocks of digital images. Each pixel stores one sample of color. To represent colors, we use color models like RGB that combine primary colors at different intensities.

exercises.question: What is a pixel?
exercises.answer: The smallest unit of a digital image, a single sample of color
exercises.explain: A pixel is one dot of color. Millions of pixels arranged in a grid form a complete image. Resolution measures image dimensions in pixels.
choices: The smallest unit of a digital image, a single sample of color

exercises.question: What does 'screen resolution' mean?
exercises.answer: The number of pixels displayed horizontally and vertically
exercises.explain: Resolution like 1920x1080 means 1920 pixels wide and 1080 pixels tall. Higher resolution means more pixels and sharper images.
choices: The distance from your eyes to the screen
The number of pixels displayed horizontally and vertically

exercises.question: What is pixel density (measured in PPI)?
exercises.answer: The number of pixels per inch on a screen
exercises.explain: PPI (pixels per inch) measures how densely packed pixels are. Retina displays have higher PPI, making images look sharper and text crisper.
choices: The refresh rate of the display
How many colors a pixel can show
The number of pixels per inch on a screen

exercises.question: What is 'sub-pixel rendering'?
exercises.answer: Using individual color components of pixels to improve text clarity
exercises.explain: Sub-pixel rendering uses the red, green, and blue parts of pixels separately to smooth text edges. It makes text appear smoother on some displays.
choices: Removing some pixels from an image
Using individual color components of pixels to improve text clarity

exercises.question: Why do 4K monitors display sharper text than 1080p?
exercises.answer: They have more pixels per inch, allowing smoother curves and edges
exercises.explain: 4K (3840x2160) has four times the pixels of 1080p (1920x1080). More pixels means finer detail, smoother text, and less pixelation.
choices: They have more pixels per inch, allowing smoother curves and edges
They refresh at a higher rate
They use a different color model
They use a special font technology

exercises.question: What is the RGB color model?
exercises.answer: A color model using Red, Green, and Blue values to create any color
exercises.explain: RGB combines red, green, and blue light at different intensities (0-255 each). Together they can create over 16 million colors.
choices: A color model using Red, Green, and Blue values to create any color
A color model using only primary pigments

exercises.question: How many distinct colors can RGB represent with 8 bits per channel?
exercises.explain: Each channel (R, G, B) has 8 bits, allowing 256 values (0-255). Total combinations: 256 x 256 x 256 = 16,777,216 colors.

exercises.question: What is the RGBA color model?
exercises.answer: RGB plus an Alpha channel for transparency
exercises.explain: RGBA adds an Alpha channel (0-255) that controls opacity. Alpha 255 is fully opaque, alpha 0 is fully transparent.
choices: RGB with a Red intensity multiplier
A system using only primary colors
RGB plus an Alpha channel for transparency

exercises.question: What is the HSL color model?
exercises.answer: A model using Hue, Saturation, and Lightness for intuitive color selection
exercises.explain: HSL separates color (hue), intensity (saturation), and brightness (lightness). It matches how humans think about colors.
choices: A model based on printing inks
A model using Hue, Saturation, and Lightness for intuitive color selection

exercises.question: What does it mean to 'dither' an image?
exercises.answer: Add controlled noise to simulate more colors with fewer bits
exercises.explain: Dithering mixes colors to make images look better when limited to fewer colors. It was essential for old displays with limited color depth.
choices: Add controlled noise to simulate more colors with fewer bits

units.title: Coordinate Systems and Transforms
units.tip: Everything in computer graphics lives in a coordinate system. Points are located by x, y (and z in 3D). Transforms like translation, rotation, and scaling move and change objects mathematically.

exercises.question: What does the origin (0, 0) represent in a 2D coordinate system?
exercises.answer: The reference point where the x and y axes meet
exercises.explain: The origin is the starting point for all coordinates. In screen graphics, it is often the top-left corner; in math, it is at the center.
choices: The reference point where the x and y axes meet

exercises.question: What is a translation transform?
exercises.answer: Moving an object by adding an offset to all its coordinates
exercises.explain: Translation shifts an object's position. To move a point (x, y) by 10 units right and 20 units down, add 10 to x and 20 to y.
choices: Making an object larger or smaller
Spinning an object around a center point
Moving an object by adding an offset to all its coordinates

exercises.question: What is a rotation transform?
exercises.answer: Spinning an object around a pivot point by a given angle
exercises.explain: Rotation uses trigonometry to spin points around a center. A 90-degree rotation turns an object clockwise or counterclockwise.
choices: Changing the size of an object
Spinning an object around a pivot point by a given angle
Moving an object to a new position
Reflecting an object across a line

exercises.question: What is a scale transform?
exercises.answer: Making an object larger or smaller by multiplying coordinates
exercises.explain: Scaling multiplies each coordinate by a factor. Multiply by 2 to make it twice as large; multiply by 0.5 to make it half as large.
choices: Making an object larger or smaller by multiplying coordinates

exercises.question: What is non-uniform scaling?
exercises.answer: Applying different scale factors to different axes
exercises.explain: Non-uniform scaling allows different amounts of stretching in different directions. Scale x by 2 and y by 0.5 to make an object wider and shorter.
choices: Applying different scale factors to different axes

exercises.question: What is the z-axis in 3D graphics?
exercises.answer: The axis perpendicular to the screen, pointing toward and away from the viewer
exercises.explain: The z-axis extends into or out of the screen. Positive z often points toward the viewer; negative z points away.
choices: The axis perpendicular to the screen, pointing toward and away from the viewer
The axis running top to bottom
The axis running left to right

exercises.question: What is perspective projection?
exercises.answer: A 3D-to-2D projection where distant objects appear smaller
exercises.explain: Perspective makes distant objects appear smaller, like railroad tracks converging at the horizon. It creates realistic depth.
choices: Showing the inside of a 3D object
A 3D-to-2D projection where distant objects appear smaller
Making all objects the same size

exercises.question: What is orthographic projection?
exercises.answer: A 3D-to-2D projection where distance does not affect size
exercises.explain: Orthographic projection ignores depth; objects stay the same size regardless of distance. It is common in technical drawings and CAD.
choices: A projection where all objects are tilted
A 3D-to-2D projection where distance does not affect size
A projection that shows only 2D objects

exercises.question: What is a camera in 3D graphics?
exercises.answer: A virtual viewpoint and projection that defines what the viewer sees
exercises.explain: A camera has a position, direction, and field of view. It defines which part of the 3D world gets rendered to the 2D screen.
choices: A virtual viewpoint and projection that defines what the viewer sees

exercises.question: What is the field of view (FOV) of a camera?
exercises.answer: The angular width and height of the area the camera can see
exercises.explain: FOV is measured in degrees. A wide FOV (120 degrees) shows more of the scene; narrow FOV (30 degrees) shows less, like a telephoto lens.
choices: The distance from the camera to the nearest object
The color of the camera's background
The angular width and height of the area the camera can see

units.title: The Rendering Pipeline
units.tip: Rendering is the process that converts 3D scene data into a 2D image on your screen. The pipeline has distinct stages: vertices are positioned, geometry is rasterized into fragments, and fragments become final pixels.

exercises.question: What is a vertex in 3D graphics?
exercises.answer: A point in 3D space with position, color, and texture data
exercises.explain: Vertices are the corners of 3D shapes. A triangle has 3 vertices; a cube has 8. Each vertex can store additional data like color or texture coordinates.
choices: A point in 3D space with position, color, and texture data
A single pixel on the screen

exercises.question: What is a primitive in graphics?
exercises.answer: A basic geometric shape like a triangle or line
exercises.explain: Primitives are the building blocks of 3D graphics. Triangles are the most common; lines, points, and quads are also used.
choices: A basic geometric shape like a triangle or line

exercises.question: Why are triangles the most common primitive?
exercises.answer: They are guaranteed to be flat and can approximate any surface
exercises.explain: Triangles are planar (always flat), making them fast to process. Curved surfaces can be approximated using many triangles.
choices: They are the only shape that can be textured
They render faster than other primitives
They are guaranteed to be flat and can approximate any surface

exercises.question: What does the vertex shader do?
exercises.answer: Transforms each vertex position, for example from model space into camera and clip space
exercises.explain: The vertex shader runs once per vertex. It applies transformations such as rotation, translation and scaling, and positions the vertex relative to the camera.
choices: Transforms each vertex position, for example from model space into camera and clip space

exercises.question: What is a mesh in 3D graphics?
exercises.answer: A collection of vertices and triangles forming a 3D object
exercises.explain: A mesh is made of triangles connected at shared vertices. A 3D model is a mesh; a character, building, or tree all start as meshes.
choices: A collection of vertices and triangles forming a 3D object

exercises.question: What is rasterization?
exercises.answer: Converting vector graphics (triangles) into raster data (pixels)
exercises.explain: Rasterization determines which pixels a triangle covers. It fills in the triangle's interior with fragments.
choices: Converting vector graphics (triangles) into raster data (pixels)

exercises.question: What is a fragment in the rendering pipeline?
exercises.answer: A candidate pixel that may become the final pixel if it passes tests
exercises.explain: A fragment is generated for each covered pixel. It has color, depth, and other data. Tests (depth, stencil) determine if it becomes final.
choices: A candidate pixel that may become the final pixel if it passes tests

exercises.question: What does the fragment shader do?
exercises.answer: Determines the color and properties of each fragment
exercises.explain: The fragment shader runs once per fragment. It calculates final color using textures, lighting, and other material properties.
choices: Determines the color and properties of each fragment

exercises.question: What is a render target?
exercises.answer: A buffer where rendered output is written
exercises.explain: A render target receives the final pixel colors. The most common target is the framebuffer displayed on your monitor.
choices: A buffer where rendered output is written

exercises.question: What is the framebuffer?
exercises.answer: The memory buffer that holds the current frame being displayed
exercises.explain: The framebuffer stores color, depth, and other data for every pixel on screen. After rendering, it is displayed by the monitor.
choices: The memory buffer that holds the current frame being displayed

units.title: Textures, Lighting, and Shading
units.tip: Textures are images applied to 3D surfaces. Lighting calculations simulate how light bounces off objects. Shading determines the color of each pixel based on surface properties and lighting.

exercises.question: What is a texture in graphics?
exercises.answer: An image applied to a 3D surface to add detail
exercises.explain: Textures are 2D images that map onto 3D geometry. A wood texture makes a polygon look like wood; a bump map adds surface detail.
choices: An image applied to a 3D surface to add detail

exercises.question: What are UV coordinates?
exercises.answer: 2D coordinates that map a texture image onto 3D geometry
exercises.explain: UV (or texture coordinates) tell the GPU where each vertex picks its color from a texture. U and V range from 0 to 1.
choices: 2D coordinates that map a texture image onto 3D geometry

exercises.question: What is texture filtering?
exercises.answer: A technique to interpolate texture colors when sampling between pixels
exercises.explain: When a texture pixel (texel) does not align with screen pixels, filtering interpolates nearby texels for smoother results.
choices: A technique to interpolate texture colors when sampling between pixels

exercises.question: What is mipmapping?
exercises.answer: Creating smaller versions of a texture for distant objects
exercises.explain: Mipmaps are downsampled copies of a texture. Distant geometry uses smaller mips for efficiency and to avoid aliasing.
choices: Creating smaller versions of a texture for distant objects

exercises.question: What does a normal map do?
exercises.answer: Encodes surface normal directions to simulate surface detail without more geometry
exercises.explain: A normal map stores surface slopes as RGB colors. It makes flat polygons appear bumpy without needing more triangles.
choices: Encodes surface normal directions to simulate surface detail without more geometry
Maps a regular texture onto a surface
Controls how light reflects off a surface

exercises.question: What is a light source in graphics?
exercises.answer: An object that emits light and affects how surfaces appear
exercises.explain: Lights have position, direction, color, and intensity. The rendering algorithm calculates how light from these sources illuminates surfaces.
choices: A color applied to the entire scene
A texture applied to a surface
An object that emits light and affects how surfaces appear

exercises.question: What is the Phong reflection model?
exercises.answer: A model that combines ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting
exercises.explain: Phong lighting has three components: ambient (overall brightness), diffuse (light hitting the surface), and specular (shiny highlights).
choices: A model that combines ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting

exercises.question: What is ambient lighting?
exercises.answer: Lighting that affects all surfaces equally, with no direction
exercises.explain: Ambient light has no direction; it illuminates the scene uniformly. Without it, areas not hit by direct light would be completely black.
choices: Lighting that affects all surfaces equally, with no direction
Light that comes from a single point

exercises.question: What is diffuse lighting?
exercises.answer: Lighting based on the angle between the surface normal and light direction
exercises.explain: Diffuse lighting makes surfaces brighter when facing the light and darker when facing away. The amount depends on the angle.
choices: Light that only appears on shiny surfaces
Lighting based on the angle between the surface normal and light direction

exercises.question: What is specular lighting?
exercises.answer: Bright highlights that appear on shiny surfaces reflecting light toward the viewer
exercises.explain: Specular highlights appear on glossy surfaces when they reflect light toward the viewer. Rough surfaces have diffuse light; shiny surfaces have specular highlights.
choices: The overall brightness of a surface
Bright highlights that appear on shiny surfaces reflecting light toward the viewer

units.title: Depth, Ray Tracing, and Anti-Aliasing
units.tip: The depth buffer prevents objects in front from being hidden by objects behind them. Ray tracing simulates realistic light behavior. Anti-aliasing removes jagged edges caused by pixelation.

lessons.title: The Depth Buffer and Rendering Order

exercises.question: What is the depth buffer (z-buffer)?
exercises.answer: A buffer that stores the depth of each pixel to determine visibility
exercises.explain: The depth buffer stores z-values (distance from camera) for each pixel. When rendering, pixels are only drawn if they are closer than the stored value.
choices: A buffer that stores the depth of each pixel to determine visibility

exercises.question: What is the depth test?
exercises.answer: A comparison that determines if a new fragment is closer than the existing pixel
exercises.explain: The depth test checks if a new fragment's depth is less than the stored depth. If yes, the fragment replaces the pixel; if no, it is discarded.
choices: A comparison that determines if a new fragment is closer than the existing pixel

exercises.question: What is the 'near plane' and 'far plane' of a camera?
exercises.answer: The closest and farthest distances from the camera that can be rendered
exercises.explain: The near plane (e.g., 0.1) is the closest objects can be to the camera. The far plane (e.g., 1000) is where objects become too distant to render.
choices: The left and right sides of the screen
The closest and farthest distances from the camera that can be rendered
The top and bottom of the camera's view

exercises.question: What is 'z-fighting'?
exercises.answer: Visual artifacts when two surfaces are at nearly the same depth
exercises.explain: Z-fighting occurs when depth precision is too low to distinguish which surface is in front. The depth buffer flickers between them.
choices: Visual artifacts when two surfaces are at nearly the same depth

exercises.question: How are transparent objects usually handled alongside depth testing?
exercises.answer: They are sorted and drawn back to front after opaque objects, using blending
exercises.explain: Blending combines a transparent fragment with what is already behind it, so transparent objects are usually drawn after opaque ones, from farthest to nearest, for correct results.
choices: They are ignored by the depth buffer and never drawn
They are removed from the scene before rendering
They are sorted and drawn back to front after opaque objects, using blending
They are drawn first, in any order

exercises.question: What is ray tracing?
exercises.answer: A rendering technique that simulates light rays bouncing around a scene
exercises.explain: Ray tracing fires rays from the camera through each pixel. It calculates reflections, refractions, and shadows by tracing rays to light sources.
choices: A rendering technique that simulates light rays bouncing around a scene

exercises.question: How does ray tracing differ from rasterization?
exercises.answer: Ray tracing simulates light realistically; rasterization is faster but less accurate
exercises.explain: Rasterization renders from objects to the screen (fast, standard). Ray tracing renders from the camera through pixels (slow, but more realistic).
choices: Ray tracing simulates light realistically; rasterization is faster but less accurate

exercises.question: What is aliasing in graphics?
exercises.answer: Jagged, stair-step edges on curved lines and polygon edges
exercises.explain: Aliasing occurs because pixels are discrete squares. Curved or diagonal lines appear jagged when drawn with pixels.
choices: Jagged, stair-step edges on curved lines and polygon edges
Too many triangles in a scene

exercises.question: What is anti-aliasing?
exercises.answer: A technique to reduce jagged edges by averaging colors over a pixel area
exercises.explain: Anti-aliasing smooths edges, often by sampling several points per pixel and blending them. Common methods include FXAA, MSAA, and TAA.
choices: A technique to reduce jagged edges by averaging colors over a pixel area

exercises.question: What is MSAA (Multisample Anti-Aliasing)?
exercises.answer: Rendering at a higher quality by sampling multiple points per pixel
exercises.explain: MSAA (2x, 4x, 8x) renders multiple samples per pixel and averages them. It reduces jagged edges with reasonable performance cost.
choices: Rendering at a higher quality by sampling multiple points per pixel
